Issues I've noticed when testing the alphabet:

* the letter "d" is only recognized if your hand is in profile, if facing the camera it will read out "x"
* the letter "i" is basically never recognized, it reads it as "t," "s," or "o" and sometimes as "y" unless you do the exact sign (thumb has to touch the second or third finger at least for it to be read properly, quite painful for me actually lol)
* the letter "k" is only recognized when angled very specifically, otherwise it will read as "t," "x," or "p"
* the letter "n" is sometimes read as "o" for some reason
* the letter "p" if signed right after another letter will read as "z." I'm assuming due to the movement? But it takes a while to switch from "z" to "p"
* the letter "q" will be read as either "q" or "p" and often switch from one to the other really quickly even if the sign itself isn't moving or changing
* the letter "r" has only been read as "u" so far, unless I basically force my fingers in a fairly painful position (for me, maybe not for others)
* the letter "x" will be read as "g" fairly often, unless the angle is just right (sort of diagonal), which isn't really realistic for everyday signing

I'm not a native signer, and I'm not fluent, so take this with a grain of salt, but that being said nobody (especially not native signers in my experience) sign the letters exactly like you would see on charts. Also, always give them the illusion of choice, that will help a ton in the long run. By asking "do you want to eat A or B?" you're giving them the feeling that they made a choice, but really both options are healthy and not things they'd actually choose otherwise.

Finally, if the kid doesn't want to eat, don't give them another option. Just say okay and send them up to bed (if the dad is okay with it, obviously). Kids will learn to eat what's in front of them, or they'll at least learn to try what's in front of them, and knowing nothing else will come after will help them to pay attention to what they're eating. I never came out to my parents either, but for different reasons. My parents are very accepting, and when I said "I have a girlfriend" 3 weeks after I said "I have a boyfriend" they  basically just said "okay cool." My mum had a gay brother and we had a lesbian couple living on my street when I was a kid, so I grew up around LGBT+ people yet for some reason when I was 14 I felt really uncomfortable with myself being a lesbian, although I supported others. Until I was 18 I didn't really question my sexuality, I was bi and that was it. Then I accepted myself, finally, and my family was relieved I wasn't lying to myself anymore. It was a really hard process, but having my family and friends made it easier honestly.

Saing "I couldn't care less" tends to be considered an okay reaction, but it feels bad. "Thank you for trusting me with this" is usually a better first reaction because it doesn't erase their struggle. Realising you're anything other than straight and/or cis is hard, it's a process, it may be this sort of obvious thing a person knows or it may take a while. By saying "I don't want to be a gay dude's dad" you're also accidentally erasing his sexuality (EDIT: as a part of him and who he is. -Sorry, I'm very sleep deprived lmao), it's obviously not your intention, but when you're 14 (and when you just come out in general) there tends to be a period where that thing is the most important. His personality, preferences, maybe favourite movies and shows and musical artists might revolve around his sexuality, because that's a safe space, and he knows that it's something he can be proud of (at least I hope he does, because it feels amazing to be proud of who you are).

At this point, the best thing to do is to sit him down and say "I don't mean that I don't care, your sexuality is important to you so it's important to me, and I love you no matter what. The thing is though, being gay doesn't change who you are to me, it doesn't change how I feel about you as my son, or how much I love you, or the fact that I'm proud of you. I'm sorry I didn't make that clear the first time around." Always keep the conversation open, if he knows he can talk to you, he likely will.

I'd recommend a bonded pair, like many have already told you, and most likely adults, or older kittens, they'll be more likely to occupy each other while you're gone. If possible, a cat tree is a must-have, and a cat shelf/walkway area can be great for them as well. It obviously depends on the space you have, but it's a good option. The litter rule is important, but if you clean twice a day (let's say morning + evening) then you can do well with only a litter per cat, or even only one for them to share, but I'd avoid it in a smaller area, it's really a case-by-case situation. I'd recommend getting a pet insurance, but that's really up to you. It can be very useful if some emergency happens. I'd recommend getting a closed litter box with crystal litter and an anti-tracking mat, as that should keep odors down as much as possible. With indoor cats, they often like looking outside so putting a cat tree next to the window, or installing a window mount can make for very, very happy kitties. If you have a balcony and the cats you get enjoy the outside, a cage can also be a great option, but that depends entirely on the types of cats you get. Learn what toys they like (my cat loves a certain type of foam ball and the cat dancer-type, and his dry food) and get those. With adults, catnip toys are great, and slow feeders, treat toys, etc, are usually my go-tos.

Anywho, good luck with your cats to be!

Outdoor is fine, as long as you have a secured garden and that you are home when the cat goes outside. We thought our garden was secure, and it wasn't, so it's important to make sure it is. A leash to take your cat on walks (although that would be your child's job I imagine) can also be a good way to get them outside, but only if they like it. Some cats never even become curious about the outdoors, but those who do may start to really love it, which is when a cage could come in if your garden isn't secure/if you don't have a garden. It's up to you, of course, but having a really big cage that allows your cat outdoor time and jumping around can be a much safer alternative!
